lessons.title: Why Companies Give Employees a Share of Ownership

children.text: On 13 November 2024, Swiggy listed on the NSE and BSE. For most investors it was one more IPO. For thousands of Swiggy employees it was the day years of stock options finally had a market price. Delivery-app engineers, product managers and operations leads, many of whom had taken lower salaries to join a loss-making startup, suddenly held something they could sell.
That is the promise of an
ESOP
. This lesson answers the first question anyone should ask about it: why would a company hand over a piece of itself to the people it already pays a salary?

markDefs.definition: Employee Stock Option: a right given to an employee to buy a fixed number of the company's shares at a pre-decided price in the future. It is a right, not an obligation.

stats.context: As widely reported around the November 2024 listing

body.text: A salary pays you for the work you did this month. An ESOP pays you only if the whole company becomes more valuable. That single difference explains why companies use them.

children.text: The Deal in One Sentence
An ESOP gives you the right, but not the obligation, to buy a fixed number of company shares at a fixed price, called the
exercise price
, at a future date. You earn that right gradually through
vesting
. If the share value climbs far above your exercise price, the gap is your gain. If it does not, you simply do not buy, and you lose nothing except the salary you might have earned elsewhere.

markDefs.definition: The pre-decided price per share an employee pays to convert an option into a real share. Also called the strike price or grant price.
The process by which an employee earns the right to actually use their options over time, usually in stages across three to four years.

children.text: India's Companies Act, 2013 defines it in almost exactly these terms in Section 2(37): an option given to directors, officers or employees that gives them the right to purchase or subscribe for the company's shares at a future date at a pre-determined price. The details of grants, vesting and exercise get their own lessons later in this course. For now, hold on to the core idea.
Why Companies Do It: Four Problems, One Tool
Every ESOP plan is trying to solve at least one of four business problems. Knowing which one your company is solving tells you a lot about how generous, and how realistic, its plan is.

body.caption: The four jobs an ESOP does for a company

cells: A young startup cannot match the salary a bank, an MNC or a large IT firm pays
Lower fixed pay today, with a share of the upside later
Good employees walk out for a 30% hike just as they become most useful
Options vest over years, so leaving early means leaving value behind
Employees optimise for their own targets, not for the value of the business
Their wealth now rises and falls with the company's value
Senior hires will not join an unknown company on cash alone
A credible ownership story makes the offer competitive

children.text: 1. Conserving cash

A Series A startup in Bengaluru burning ₹3 crore a month cannot pay a senior engineer ₹60 lakh in cash. It can pay ₹40 lakh and offer options that could be worth far more if the company succeeds. The company keeps cash for building the product. The employee takes a calculated bet.
2. Keeping people

Options are usually earned in stages over three to four years. If you resign after 18 months, the part that has not vested yet is typically gone. That unvested value is often called golden handcuffs: nobody forces you to stay, but leaving has a visible price.
3. Aligning interests

Shareholders want the company to be worth more. Employees, left alone, want a bigger salary and an easier target. ESOPs pull those two closer together. A customer-support lead who owns options has a personal reason to care about churn, not just ticket counts.
4. Winning talent
When Swiggy, Zomato, Razorpay or Zepto hire a senior leader from Amazon or Google, the cash component rarely wins the argument alone. The ESOP grant is often the deciding line in the offer letter.

body.title: Spot the Main Motive
body.question: A bootstrapped D2C brand in Jaipur cannot afford market salaries for its first five hires. The founder offers each of them 25% below-market pay plus stock options. Which problem is the ESOP mainly solving?
options: Complying with SEBI rules for listed companies
Conserving cash while still attracting good people
Reducing the company's income tax bill
body.explanation: The company is unlisted, so SEBI's listed-company ESOP rules are not the driver, and options guarantee nothing. The founder is swapping scarce cash today for a share of future value, which is the classic early-stage reason for ESOPs.

children.text: What It Looks Like from the Employee's Chair
Meet Ananya, a product analyst in Gurugram with two offers. A private bank offers
₹24 lakh a year in cash
. A fintech startup offers
₹18 lakh in cash plus 4,000 options at an exercise price of ₹10
, vesting over four years.
If she stays four years at the startup, she gives up ₹6,00,000 a year, which is ₹24,00,000 in total. Is the ESOP worth it? It depends entirely on what each share is worth when she can finally sell.

body.caption: Pre-tax gain, ignoring the time value of money. If the share value is at or below the exercise price, the gain is zero because you would not exercise.

body.title: Ananya's ESOP gain vs the cash she gave up (₹ lakh)
body.xAxisLabel: Share value when she can sell (₹)

series.label: Cash salary given up over 4 years

children.text: The share needs to be worth ₹610 just for the ESOP to match the salary she gave up. That is 61 times the exercise price. At ₹160 a share she makes ₹6,00,000, a nice sum, but still ₹18,00,000 less than taking the bank job. At ₹1,010 she is ₹16,00,000 ahead.

body.text: The question is never "How many options am I getting?" It is "What share value do I need for these options to beat the cash I am giving up, and how likely is that?"

body.title: Calculate the Gain
body.prompt: Rohit holds 2,500 vested options at an exercise price of ₹25. His company's shares are now valued at ₹145. What is his pre-tax gain if he exercises and sells at that value?
body.explanation: Gain per option = ₹145 minus ₹25 = ₹120. Total gain = ₹120 × 2,500 = ₹3,00,000, before any tax.

body.title: Find the Breakeven Share Value
body.prompt: Meera gives up ₹8 lakh of cash salary in total to join a startup that grants her 5,000 options at an exercise price of ₹20. Ignoring tax and time value, what share value does the company need to reach for her ESOP gain to equal the salary she gave up?
body.explanation: Gain needed per option = ₹8,00,000 ÷ 5,000 = ₹160. Add the ₹20 she must pay to exercise: breakeven share value = ₹180.

children.text: Cash vs Options: An Honest Comparison

columns.label: Cash salary
points: Certain: credited to your account every month
Spendable immediately for EMIs, rent and SIPs
Taxed as salary in the year you receive it
Worth the same whether the company soars or struggles
Stays with you when you resign

columns.label: ESOPs
points: Uncertain: could be worth crores or nothing
Usually cannot be sold until a liquidity event
Taxed in stages, at exercise and again at sale
Value depends entirely on how the company performs
Unvested options are normally lost when you leave

children.text: It Is Not Just a Startup Thing

Startups made ESOPs famous, but large listed companies use them too, mainly to retain senior talent and share wealth with the people who build it. The story in India starts well before the startup boom.

body.title: ESOP moments that shaped Indian corporate culture

events.title: Infosys spreads ownership widely
events.description: Infosys ran stock option plans that reached far beyond senior management. By the end of the decade, hundreds of employees had become crorepatis, and the "Infoscion millionaire" became a symbol of what ESOPs could do.

events.title: Flipkart pays out $700 million
events.description: After separating from PhonePe, Flipkart paid about $700 million to current and former employees to compensate ESOP holders for the value that moved out with PhonePe.

events.title: Zomato grants about 1.2 crore options
events.description: Already listed, Zomato granted nearly 1.2 crore options to employees, worth roughly ₹330 crore at the then share price of about ₹275.

events.title: Swiggy lists on NSE and BSE
events.description: The IPO turned years of unlisted options held by thousands of employees into shares with a daily market price.

events.title: Flipkart announces a $50 million buyback
events.description: Eligible employees could sell up to 5% of their vested options back to the company, a liquidity route for a company that is still unlisted.

body.label: Zomato ESOP grant, October 2024
body.context: Nearly 1.2 crore options, valued at a BSE closing price of ₹275.20. A listed company using ESOPs to retain talent as competition heated up.

children.text: The Catch: Paper Wealth Is Not Money
Every rupee figure in a startup ESOP story is
paper wealth
until there is a
liquidity event
. Three things can go wrong between the grant letter and your bank account:

markDefs.definition: Wealth that exists only as a valuation on paper. It becomes real money only when the shares can actually be sold.
An event that lets employees turn their shares or options into cash, such as an IPO, a company buyback of employee options, or a sale of the company.

children.text: The company fails or its valuation falls.
If shares end up worth less than the exercise price, the options are worthless.
There is no buyer for years.
An unlisted company may not IPO or run a buyback for a long time, so the options cannot be turned into cash.
You leave before vesting.
Resign early and the unvested portion usually goes back to the company.

body.text: Never accept a lower salary that stretches your monthly budget on the assumption that ESOPs will make up for it. Plan your EMIs and emergency fund on cash salary alone, and treat ESOPs as upside.

body.title: If ESOPs cost the company no cash, who actually pays for them?

children.text: The existing shareholders do. When employees exercise options, new shares are usually issued, so founders and investors each own a slightly smaller percentage. That is called
dilution
. Companies also have to record ESOPs as an expense in their accounts, even though no cash leaves the bank.

markDefs.definition: The fall in each existing shareholder's percentage ownership when a company issues new shares, including shares issued to employees who exercise options.

children.text: This is why investors watch the size of the ESOP pool closely, and why founders cannot hand out options without limit. We cover pool sizing, dilution and accounting cost in Chapter 5.

body.title: Complete the Definition
body.textWithBlank: An ESOP gives an employee the right, but not the ___, to buy company shares at a pre-decided price in the future.
body.explanation: That is exactly why it is called an option. If the share value stays below the exercise price, the employee simply does not exercise, and loses nothing out of pocket.

body.title: The Founder's Dilemma
body.scenario: Karthik runs a 40-person B2B SaaS startup in Pune that raised a seed round six months ago. He needs a head of engineering. The best candidate earns ₹55 lakh at a large MNC. Karthik can pay at most ₹38 lakh in cash without shortening the company's runway.
body.prompt: How should Karthik use ESOPs to close this hire? What should he be careful about?
body.modelAnswer: Karthik should offer ₹38 lakh in cash plus a meaningful ESOP grant that vests over about four years, so the candidate is paid for staying through the phase where they add the most value. He should explain the offer honestly: the current valuation, the total number of shares, what percentage the grant represents, and what share value would make it worth more than the ₹17 lakh a year the candidate gives up. He should be careful not to promise returns, not to size the grant so large that it drains the ESOP pool he will need for future hires, and not to leave the candidate so short of cash that personal money stress drives them out in a year anyway.

cards.definition: A right, not an obligation, to buy company shares at a fixed price in the future.
The fixed price per share you pay to turn an option into a share.
Earning the right to use your options gradually over time.
The retention effect of unvested options that you lose if you leave early.
An IPO, buyback or company sale that lets you convert options or shares into cash.
The fall in existing shareholders' percentage ownership when new shares are issued.

points: An ESOP is the right to buy company shares at a fixed exercise price in the future, earned gradually through vesting.
Companies use ESOPs to conserve cash, retain people, align employees with shareholders and win talent they cannot afford on salary alone.
Your gain is share value minus exercise price, times the number of options, and it is zero if the share value never beats the exercise price.
Always work out the breakeven share value needed to beat the cash salary you are giving up.
ESOP wealth stays on paper until a liquidity event such as an IPO, a buyback or a sale of the company.
ESOPs are not free: existing shareholders bear the cost through dilution.

body.text: This lesson is for education only. It is not investment, tax or legal advice. ESOP terms differ from company to company, so always read your own grant letter and scheme document, and consult a qualified professional before making decisions.
